extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in literary criticism and religious critique (readers of Mark Twain / critics of Christian Science)
extracted.subtask_short: literary critique of Christian Science leader
extracted.subtask_description: A journalistic/literary essay evaluating Mary Baker Eddy's character, authorship, organizational methods, and the moral/economic practices of her religious movement; combines stylistic analysis of her writings with socio-economic and institutional critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate inspiration and planning before producing 'inspired' text
rubrics_metrics.description: An inspirer should 'sit down and think it out and know what it is I want to say before I begin.' Rushed, half-digested inspiration produces slipshod work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes hurried or improvised 'inspirations' (e.g., multiple inconsistent renderings) and holds deliberate, well-considered composition as a standard; the critique implies that a genuine inspirer must be able to produce coherent, stable text rather than inconsistent revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical pricing and distribution of sacred texts
rubrics_metrics.description: If a book claims to be a divine message it should be sold at a pinched margin above cost to those who can pay and given free to those who cannot (as Bible societies do).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author contrasts Bible societies (offering whole Bible for 15¢, New Testament for 5¢) with Mrs. Eddy's Science and Health (sold at $3–$6), arguing that charging large profits for a purportedly divine message is morally wrong; this is presented as a standard for how religious works ought to be distributed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and fairness in canvassing / sales practices for religious books
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious leaders/publishers should not exploit canvassers or coerce sales; issuance of orders to 'circulate and sell as many of these books as they can' (and threats like excommunication for noncompliance) is unethical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites the command in the Christian Science Journal and a By-law threatening loss of membership for failing to obey, presenting this as an abusive, coercive canvassing system and a standard-violating practice compared to voluntary, low-cost dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing competence: grammar, clarity, literary precision, and lucidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Good authorship requires more than commercial skill: correct grammar, a keen sense of word values, literary precision, and the ability to put thoughts into words lucidly so readers understand them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author repeatedly fault-finds Mrs. Eddy's known writings as 'third-rate English,' weak in grammar, lacking precision, and often obscure; he suggests comparing a labored Preface with a lucid chapter to test for authorship and uses that contrast as an evaluative method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use internal stylistic/textual evidence to assess authorship claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorship can be judged by comparing stylistic features (e.g., sentence construction, clarity) across texts; marked differences suggest multiple hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic recommends dissecting sentences of the Preface and comparing them with other chapters (e.g., the chapter on 'Prayer') to determine if they could plausibly be by the same author; this is offered as a practical forensic criterion for attributing authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor concrete acts and verifiable facts over unsupported assertions when judging character
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating a person, weight should be given to consistent, verifiable actions rather than to their spoken assertions, which may be unsupported or unstable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay contrasts Mrs. Eddy's talk (characterized as 'unsupported assertion' and unstable) with her acts (consistent and reliably reflective of her nature), recommending that observers rely on deeds as more trustworthy evidence of character and intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess leadership by concentration and exercise of organizational power
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate a religious leader by the offices/roles they hold and the degree of centralized control (e.g., titles, proprietary claims, sole doctrinal authority, control of appointments and excommunication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author lists numerous official-sounding positions held or claimed (President, Treasurer, Proprietor of Publishing, Sole Expondent of Doctrine, etc.) and uses the enumeration as a metric of her practical authority and despotism; he also explains how By-laws and personal reservations affect institutional succession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traits that indicate effective movement-building or religious entrepreneurship
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful founders often display business acumen: clear head for business, accurate estimation of opportunity, intelligence in planning, firmness, daring, indestructible persistence, ambition, and knowledge of human weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic enumerates these qualities (and notes 'limitless selfishness' and 'never-wavering confidence') as the capacities that enabled Mrs. Eddy's rise, presenting them as a checklist for judging whether an individual has the temperament and skills to build and consolidate a religious movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeptical standard for claimed divine originality (questions of borrowing, authorship, and invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge claims of unique divine revelation by asking whether the ideas were borrowed (from figures like Quimby), carried in manuscript, independently discovered, philosophized, written down by the claimant, and whether the claimant (not another) built and organized the religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay explicitly lists five questions about origin and authorship of the 'Great Idea' (did she borrow it, how did she get it, did she hit upon it herself, did she systematize and write it, did she build the religion herself) and treats affirmative, evidential answers as necessary to accept claims of originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat follower testimony as prejudiced when worship is present
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimonies from devotees who worship the leader are inherently biased and should be discounted or treated with caution in assessing the leader's character or originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that worship 'does not question nor criticize' and that admirers sincerely believe in the leader's sinlessness and inspiration; therefore their accounts are not reliable independent evidence and must be balanced against critical inquiry.
